edges.label: The topic 'Comparisons' introduces comparison_operators.
wrong: Writes =< or => instead of <= and >=. | right: The operators are written <= and >=.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in maths = states that two things are equal, and inequalities can be chained (a < b < c) or spoken as 'equal or less than' (=<). Java rule: = assigns while == compares; the operators are spelled <= and >= only; a < b < c does not compile; and on Strings == compares references.
[1] misconception (M) -> ChainedComparison: wrong rule: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100. Right rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.
[2] misconception (M) -> EqualityOperatorComparesObjectsValues: wrong rule: == compares the contents of two Strings. Right rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; "abc" == "ab" + x is false even when x is "c"; s.equals(t) compares the text.
[3] misconception (M) -> StringRelationalComparison: wrong rule: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically. Right rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile (use s.compareTo(t)).
[4] misconception (M) -> LessGreaterSwapped: wrong rule: < and > mean the same thing (or a < b means a is greater than b). Right rule: a < b is true when a is smaller than b; a > b when a is larger.
[5] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ChainedComparison: Points to LT (evaluate both operands, promote to a common type, then compare). Applied unevenly: the student treats < as <= on the boundary pass of a loop, or compares an int with a double as ints on one line and as doubles on another. (here mixing in: "90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100")
[6] misconception (M) -> AssignCompares: wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them and produces a boolean.
[7] misconception (M) -> ComparisonWithBooleanLiteral: wrong rule: You must write == true / == false to test a boolean. Right rule: if (b) already tests b, so writing == true adds nothing.
[8] misconception (M) -> EqualsComparesReferences: wrong rule: .equals() compares references, not contents. Right rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters; it is == that compares references.

[0] names_the_element (N): Comparison (relational) operators ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= are mixed-type operators: they take two operands of a numeric type and produce a boolean.
[1] states_the_rule (S): ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= are defined for each primitive numeric type and produce a boolean; they have lower precedence than arithmetic and higher than boolean operators; < and > are not defined for Strings, and == on non-primitive types compares identity.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Evaluate the left operand (including its arithmetic), then the right operand; if their types differ, promote the narrower one (int to double); then compare and produce true or false.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The result is a boolean: (2 <= 2) is true, 2 < 2 is false, (x < 3.1) is true for int x = 3; any comparison involving NaN, even NaN == NaN, is false.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): A comparison changes no variable and only returns a boolean, unlike =, which changes the value of the variable on its left.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): A comparison is itself an expression whose value is a boolean, so it can appear anywhere a boolean is needed, including on the right of an assignment (boolean ok = x > y;).
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Comparisons are the building blocks of conditions: together with boolean logic they provide the basis for decision-making.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): Comparisons bind tighter than && and ||, so they are evaluated first and logical operators combine their boolean results.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): Comparisons take numbers and produce a boolean; boolean values themselves can be compared only with == and != (not <), and testing them against true is unnecessary.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
[5] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Used to test a numeric condition: thresholds and sign checks, range tests, divisibility (n % k == 0), loop continuation (i < N), sentinel checks, and running-extreme updates (if (x > max) max = x).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ChainedComparison: Changing < to <= (or > to >=) changes the result only at the boundary value, which in a loop guard means one more or one fewer iteration (off-by-one); mirroring the comparison (a < b to b > a) preserves the value; negating it gives the complementary operator (!(a < b) is a >= b).
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The operators are written <= and >=. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Writing =< or => (e.g. if (x => 0)).
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use comparison operators for numeric and char tests; for Strings use equals (or compareTo); for computed doubles use a tolerance; for booleans use the variable itself instead of == true.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: == compares, = assigns. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: if (a = b) with int operands (with boolean operands it compiles and silently assigns).
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: == on Strings compares references, not text. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Comparing a String built at run time (input, concatenation) with a literal using ==.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparisons cannot be chained; both operands must be compatible. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: s < t on Strings, a < b < c, or 5 < "6".
[6] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Computed doubles should not be compared with ==. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: == between doubles produced by arithmetic, e.g. (0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 == 0.3).

x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
Relational operators compare two numbers to give a boolean; logical operators combine booleans into one boolean.
A comparison such as a < b takes two numbers and produces a boolean result.
A comparison such as x < y produces a boolean result; comparisons together with boolean logic provide the basis for decision-making.
Comparison operators build expressions whose value is a boolean, so one must already know what an expression is to understand a < b.
